mainTopic: Is a cooked untorn udder permitted, how is it torn, and may it be roasted without tearing?
overview: The משנה says that someone who cooks an udder without tearing it open first 'does not violate' the ban on בשר בחלב. In one version, רבי זירא quotes רב that the udder is fully permitted. In a second version, רב says it is still rabbinically forbidden. In both versions the גמרא tests רב against the משנה's wording and against a ברייתא about tearing the heart, and each source can be read either way. A ברייתא then supports the first version: an udder cooked in its milk is permitted, but a stomach cooked with its milk is forbidden, because the stomach's milk was collected inside the animal. רב יהודה requires a cross-shaped tear and pressing the udder against a wall, while a story about רבי אלעזר shows that a simple tear is enough. ילתא tells רב נחמן that for everything the Torah forbade, it permitted something similar, and asks for a taste of meat with milk. רב נחמן has udders roasted for her. The גמרא explains that tearing is needed only for a pot, and that roasting an untorn udder is allowed even from the start. The explanation of that wording continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רב: The untorn udder is fully permitted
steps.stepSummary: רב, quoted by רבי זירא, rules that an udder cooked without being torn is not a Torah violation and is completely permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: רבי זירא said in the name of רב: He does not violate the prohibition, and the food is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with רב's explanation of the משנה about an udder that was cooked without first being torn open. רב says the person does not violate the prohibition, and the food is completely allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only said 'he does not violate it'. רב adds a key word: 'and it is permitted'. That means there is no Torah prohibition and no rabbinic prohibition either, so the food may be eaten even לכתחילה.

keyTerms.meaning: Udder, the part of the animal that holds milk
He does not violate it, meaning he breaks no Torah prohibition
And it is permitted, meaning fully allowed

phrases.aramaic: גְּמָ׳ אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: GEMARA: Rabbi Zeira said that Rav said:
He does not violate it, and it is permitted.
phrases.notes: 'It' is the ban on meat and milk. The case is an udder that was cooked while still full of its milk.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה's case of the udder.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An udder cooked without tearing involves no Torah violation and is fully permitted, with no rabbinic prohibition either.

steps.title: The משנה's wording suggests a lesser prohibition remains
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב: the משנה's words 'does not violate' imply only that there is no Torah violation, so a rabbinic prohibition still applies.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't we learn in the משנה: 'He does not violate it'? That means it is only a Torah violation that he does not commit, but a prohibition still exists!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב's ruling from the exact wording of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the food were fully permitted, the משנה should have said 'it is permitted'. By saying only 'he does not violate it', it seems to mean there is no Torah violation but there is still a rabbinic ban. That directly contradicts רב's word 'מותר'.

keyTerms.meaning: To violate, meaning to break a Torah prohibition
There is a prohibition, meaning a lesser, rabbinic one
But isn't it so: introduces a challenge

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא אֲנַן תְּנַן אֵינוֹ עוֹבֵר עָלָיו –
phrases.english: But didn't we learn: 'He does not violate it'?
It is only violating that he does not do,
but a prohibition does exist!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's ruling in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that the untorn udder is fully permitted (מותר).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's limited phrase 'does not violate' implies that a rabbinic prohibition remains, which contradicts 'permitted'.

steps.title: The wording was borrowed from the heart case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that really there is no prohibition at all for the udder. The משנה used 'does not violate' only to match the next case, the heart, where an eating prohibition does remain.
steps.simpleTranslation: By right, there is no prohibition at all here either. But since the משנה wanted to teach in the later case: 'The heart: one tears it and removes its blood; if he did not tear it, he does not violate it', and there he is exempt from the specified punishment, but an eating prohibition does exist, the משנה also taught the first case with the words 'he does not violate it'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב by explaining why the משנה chose the words 'does not violate' even for a case that is fully permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the heart case, the phrase limits punishment, not all prohibition. Rashi explains that the blood is less than a כזית, so there are no lashes, but a half-measure remains forbidden by Torah law. The משנה borrowed the same phrase for the udder, even though Rav permits the udder in this version. Thus the shared wording does not disprove Rav.

keyTerms.meaning: By right, meaning it really should have been this way
Since, meaning 'because it was already saying'. Used for wording borrowed from a nearby case
The later part of a משנה
The first part of a משנה
He tears it open

steps.confusionAlert: Matching wording does not mean matching law. In this version Rav permits the udder, while the heart still has an eating prohibition. Rashi calls the half-measure of blood forbidden by Torah law.

phrases.english: By right, there is no prohibition either,
but since it wanted to teach the later clause:
'The heart: he tears it and removes its blood;
if he did not tear it, he does not violate it.'
There, it is only violating that he does not do,
but a prohibition does exist,

phrases.aramaic: תְּנָא נָמֵי רֵישָׁא אֵינוֹ עוֹבֵר עָלָיו.
phrases.english: so it also taught the first clause as 'he does not violate it.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Matching wording: the phrase in the first case is borrowed from the second case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase 'does not violate' in the udder case means a rabbinic prohibition remains.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase is exact only in the heart case. In the udder case it was used to match the style, and the udder is fully permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common pattern: a משנה may use the same phrase for neighboring cases even when only one case needs that exact meaning.

steps.title: Attempted support from a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tries to prove רב right from a ברייתא that requires tearing the heart after cooking but says nothing similar about the udder.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say a ברייתא supports רב: 'The udder: one tears it and removes its milk; if he did not tear it, he does not violate it. The heart: one tears it and removes its blood; if he did not tear it, he tears it after cooking, and it is permitted.' So only the heart needs tearing afterward, but the udder needs no tearing at all, meaning it is permitted as is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests that a ברייתא backs up רב's ruling that the udder is fully permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives a fix for the heart: tear it after cooking. It gives no fix for the udder. The suggested reading is that the udder needs no fix because it is already completely permitted, just as רב said.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say it supports him? This opens an attempted proof
After it was cooked
Tearing open
Needs, requires

phrases.english: Shall we say this supports him:
phrases.notes: 'Him' is רב, and the source quoted next is a ברייתא.

phrases.english: 'The udder: he tears it and removes its milk;
if he did not tear it, he does not violate it.
The heart: he tears it and removes its blood;

phrases.aramaic: לֹא קְרָעוֹ – קוֹרְעוֹ לְאַחַר בִּשּׁוּלוֹ וּמוּתָּר.
phrases.english: if he did not tear it, he tears it after cooking, and it is permitted.'
It is the heart that needs tearing,
but the udder does not need tearing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רב, the גמרא now looks for positive support for him.
steps.raayaObject: רב's ruling that the untorn cooked udder is fully permitted.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that requires tearing the heart after cooking but gives no such step for the udder.

steps.title: The ברייתא may mean the udder cannot be fixed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof: maybe the heart can be fixed by tearing it after cooking, but the udder cannot be fixed that way, so it stays forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps it is the heart for which tearing after cooking is enough, but for the udder, tearing afterward is not enough.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof by reading the ברייתא the opposite way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's silence about tearing the udder after cooking can mean two things. Either the udder needs no fix, or no fix helps it. If tearing cannot help the udder, then it is not fully permitted, so the ברייתא does not prove רב right.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps. Used to offer another reading that weakens a proof
It is enough for it

steps.whatToRemember: רב rules that the untorn udder is fully permitted. The משנה's wording does not disprove him, because it was borrowed from the heart case. But the ברייתא does not prove him right either, since it can be read to mean the udder cannot be fixed.
steps.confusionAlert: This rejection does not prove רב wrong. It only shows the ברייתא is not a clear proof for him.

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְמָא לֵב הוּא דְּסַגִּי לֵיהּ בִּקְרִיעָה,
phrases.english: Perhaps it is the heart for which tearing is enough,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל כְּחָל – לָא סַגִּי לֵיהּ בִּקְרִיעָה.
phrases.english: but for the udder, tearing is not enough.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּלְמָא לֵב הוּא דְּסַגִּי לֵיהּ בִּקְרִיעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof offered in step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the ברייתא, not רב's ruling itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof read the ברייתא's silence about the udder as 'no fix needed'. It can just as easily mean 'no fix helps', which would leave the udder forbidden.

steps.title: Second version: רב says the untorn udder is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: In a second version, רבי זירא quotes רב: cooking an untorn udder is not a Torah violation, but it is still forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say a different version: רבי זירא said in the name of רב: He does not violate a Torah law with it, but it is still forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts over with a second report of what רב said about an udder cooked without tearing. In this report, רב says it is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, רב said the udder is completely permitted. Here רב agrees there is no Torah violation, but he adds that a rabbinic prohibition still applies. Everything that follows is checked against this stricter version.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not violate a Torah prohibition with it
But it is forbidden (by rabbinic law)
Udder: the subject of רב's ruling

phrases.english: And some say:
Rabbi Zeira said that Rav said:
He does not violate a prohibition with it, but it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restarts the discussion with a second version of רב's ruling from step 1, now stricter.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An untorn udder that was cooked involves no Torah violation, but it is rabbinically forbidden.

steps.title: Trying to support רב from the משנה's wording
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the משנה's phrase 'he does not violate' supports רב, since it hints that a lesser prohibition remains.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say the משנה supports him: it says 'He does not violate with it.' This means only that he does not violate a Torah law, but a prohibition still exists.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to prove this second version of רב from the exact wording of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says 'he does not violate,' not 'it is permitted.' That wording seems to say only that there is no Torah violation, which leaves room for a rabbinic prohibition. That is exactly what רב says in this version. In step 2 this same reading was a challenge to רב. Here it works as support for him.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say it supports him: an attempted proof
To violate (a Torah law)
A prohibition (here, a rabbinic one)

phrases.english: Let us say it supports him:
"He does not violate a prohibition with it":
It is only violating a Torah law that he does not do,
but there is still a prohibition.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to back up the ruling of step 6 from the משנה's wording.
steps.raayaObject: רב's ruling (second version) that the untorn udder is rabbinically forbidden
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's wording 'אֵינוֹ עוֹבֵר עָלָיו', which suggests only that there is no Torah violation

steps.title: The משנה's wording only matches the heart case
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed away. The משנה's wording may only copy the next case, the heart, where a prohibition really remains. The udder may be fully permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, there is no prohibition at all for the udder. The משנה wanted to teach the next case: the heart is torn and its blood removed, and if he did not tear it, he does not violate. There, he is exempt from the specified punishment, but an eating prohibition exists. So the משנה used the words 'he does not violate' in the first case too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the attempted support for רב. The wording of the משנה proves nothing about the udder.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase limits punishment in the heart case, where an eating prohibition remains. Rashi explains that less than a כזית of blood has no lashes but remains forbidden by Torah law. The udder clause may borrow that wording, so the wording alone does not prove the udder forbidden. This is step 3’s explanation, now rejecting a proof rather than answering a challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: By right; strictly speaking
Since; because (it wanted to keep the wording parallel)
The latter clause of a משנה
The first clause of a משנה
Heart: needs tearing to remove its blood

phrases.english: By right, there is no prohibition either,
but since he wanted to teach the latter clause:
The heart: he tears it and removes its blood,
if he did not tear it, he does not violate a prohibition with it,
where there, he is exempt from the specified punishment,
but there is still a prohibition,
he also taught in the first clause, "He does not violate a prohibition with it."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 7 by explaining the משנה's wording another way.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from the משנה's wording; רב's ruling itself still stands
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The phrase 'he does not violate' may be borrowed from the heart case so the cases match, so it says nothing precise about the udder.

steps.title: Challenge from the ברייתא: only the heart needs tearing after cooking
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says an untorn heart must be torn after cooking, but says no such thing about the udder. This implies the udder is simply permitted, against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: The udder is torn and its milk removed. If he did not tear it, he does not violate. The heart is torn and its blood removed. If he did not tear it, he tears it after cooking and it is permitted. So only the heart needs tearing, but the udder needs no tearing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to show the cooked untorn udder is permitted. That goes against this version of רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the heart, the ברייתא demands a fix (tearing after cooking) before it may be eaten. For the udder, it demands nothing. That suggests the udder is fine as it is. If so, רב's claim that the udder is forbidden looks wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Tearing (cutting open to release milk or blood)
After its cooking
Its milk (here not forbidden fat)
And it is permitted

steps.confusionAlert: These exact lines were used in step 4 as a proof FOR רב. Now רב holds the udder is forbidden, so the same ברייתא becomes a challenge AGAINST him.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
The udder: he tears it and removes its milk,
phrases.notes: Here חֶלְבּוֹ means its milk, not forbidden fat.

phrases.english: if he did not tear it, he does not violate a prohibition with it.
The heart: he tears it and removes its blood,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא קְרָעוֹ – קוֹרְעוֹ לְאַחַר בִּשּׁוּלוֹ, וּמוּתָּר.
phrases.english: if he did not tear it, he tears it after its cooking, and it is permitted.
It is the heart that needs tearing,
but the udder does not need tearing!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הַכְּחָל – קוֹרְעוֹ וּמוֹצִיא אֶת חֶלְבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the support from the משנה failed, the גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to go against רב.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling in step 6 that the untorn udder is forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא requires a fix only for the heart. Its silence about the udder implies the udder is permitted as it is.

steps.title: Tearing can fix the heart but not the udder
steps.stepSummary: The challenge is answered. The heart can be fixed by tearing after cooking, but the udder cannot be fixed at all, so it stays forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps it is the heart for which tearing is enough, but for the udder tearing is not enough.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב by reading the ברייתא the other way around.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's silence about the udder does not mean the udder needs no fix. It may mean the udder has no fix at all. Tearing after cooking helps the heart, but it does not help the udder, so the udder remains forbidden, just as רב said. This is the same reasoning as step 5, now used to protect רב instead of to block a proof for him.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps: introduces another way to read a source
It is enough for it; it works

steps.whatToRemember: In this second version רב holds the cooked untorn udder is rabbinically forbidden. Neither the משנה's wording nor the ברייתא proves him right or wrong, because each can be read both ways. רב's ruling stands.

phrases.aramaic: דִּלְמָא לֵב הוּא דְּסַגִּי לֵיהּ בִּקְרִיעָה,
phrases.english: Perhaps it is the heart for which tearing is enough,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל כְּחָל לָא סַגִּי לֵיהּ בִּקְרִיעָה.
phrases.english: but for the udder, tearing is not enough.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּלְמָא לֵב הוּא דְּסַגִּי לֵיהּ בִּקְרִיעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 9 by reversing the inference from the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the inference drawn from the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The udder is not mentioned as needing tearing because it is permitted as it is.
steps.terutzMaskana: The udder is not mentioned as needing tearing because tearing cannot fix it, so it stays forbidden.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רב's first version
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that an udder cooked in its milk is permitted, but a stomach cooked with its milk is forbidden. It explains that the stomach's milk was collected inside the animal, while the udder's milk was not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is taught in a ברייתא, matching רב's first version: An udder cooked in its milk is permitted. A stomach cooked with its milk is forbidden. What is the difference? The stomach's milk was gathered into the animal's insides. The udder's milk was never gathered into its insides.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that agrees with רב's first version, which says a cooked untorn udder is permitted. The ברייתא also explains why an udder differs from a stomach full of milk.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 6 through 10 dealt with רב's second version, which says the udder is forbidden. This ברייתא openly says 'permitted', so it supports the first version instead. The reason given: milk a young animal drank is real milk that was collected inside it, so it is forbidden. Milk still inside the udder is treated as part of the flesh.

keyTerms.meaning: In line with the first version (of a teaching)
Udder
Stomach (of a young animal that nursed)
Difference, distinction
Gathered into its insides

steps.whatToRemember: Udder milk is treated as part of the meat, so a cooked untorn udder is permitted. Milk that collected in a stomach is real milk, so the stomach is forbidden.

phrases.english: It is taught in line with the first version of Rav:
An udder that one cooked in its milk is permitted,
a stomach that one cooked in its milk is forbidden.
phrases.notes: This means the milk a nursing calf or lamb drank, which is still sitting in its stomach.

phrases.english: And what is the difference between this and that?
This (the stomach's milk) is gathered in its insides,
and that (the udder's milk) is not gathered in its insides.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending the second version, the גמרא brings a ברייתא supporting the first version.
steps.raayaObject: רב's first version: a cooked untorn udder is permitted
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that explicitly calls the cooked udder permitted and contrasts it with a stomach

steps.title: How should the udder be torn?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what method of tearing the udder is required.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does one tear it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question: how exactly should the udder be torn before cooking? This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said to tear the udder and take out its milk, but it did not say how. The גמרא now asks what kind of tear is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: How?
He tears it

phrases.english: How does one tear it?
phrases.notes: 'It' is the udder, which the משנה says to tear before cooking.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from whether the udder is permitted to how it is properly torn.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The required method of tearing the udder

steps.title: רב יהודה: tear it crosswise and press it on a wall
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says the udder is torn lengthwise and widthwise, then pressed against a wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: One tears it lengthwise and widthwise and presses it against a wall.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers that the udder must be cut in a cross shape and then pressed against a wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a strict method. Cutting both ways and pressing the udder against a wall squeezes out as much milk as possible.

keyTerms.meaning: Lengthwise and widthwise (like warp and weft threads)
Smears or presses it against a wall

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
one tears it lengthwise and widthwise,
and presses it against a wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה קוֹרְעוֹ שְׁתִי וָעֵרֶב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Tear lengthwise and widthwise and press against a wall

steps.title: רבי אלעזר tells his attendant to tear the udder
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר tells his attendant to tear the udder for him so that he can eat it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said to his attendant: Tear it for me, and I will eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story. רבי אלעזר asked his attendant to tear an udder so he could eat it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר only says 'tear', with no mention of a cross-shaped cut or a wall. The next steps ask what this story is teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: His attendant
Tear!

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said to his attendant:
Tear it for me, and I will eat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a practical story about tearing the udder.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אלעזר ate an udder after it was simply torn

steps.title: Why tell us this? The משנה already says it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the story adds, since the משנה already says to tear the udder.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is this teaching us? It is already in the משנה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the story: the משנה already says to tear the udder, so what new thing does the story teach?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רבי אלעזר is only following the משנה, the story seems to add nothing. The גמרא wants to find a new point in it.

keyTerms.meaning: What is this teaching us?
It is (already) the משנה

phrases.english: What is it teaching us?
It is the mishna!
phrases.notes: The משנה says to tear the udder and take out its milk.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן מַתְנִיתִין הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the purpose of the story in step 14.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The story seems to repeat what the משנה already teaches.

steps.title: A simple tear is enough
steps.stepSummary: The story teaches that a cross-shaped cut and pressing against a wall are not needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us this: we do not need lengthwise and widthwise cuts and pressing it against a wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the story's new point is that a simple tear is enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rabbi Elazar’s simple tear is enough for his case. Rashi explains that this is roasting, while Rav Yehuda’s lengthwise-and-widthwise tearing applies to a pot. Rabbeinu Tam instead distinguishes a pot without meat from a pot with meat. Do not treat the two instructions as an unqualified disagreement.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us
We do not require

steps.whatToRemember: The required tearing depends on the cooking case. Rabbi Elazar’s simple tear does not cancel Rav Yehuda’s requirement in the stricter case.

phrases.english: This is what it teaches us:
that we do not require lengthwise and widthwise
and pressing it against a wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּלָא בָּעֵינַן שְׁתִי וָעֵרֶב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Finds a new point in the story
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The story only repeats the משנה's rule to tear the udder
steps.terutzMaskana: A simple tear suffices in Rabbi Elazar’s case; the stricter tearing applies in a different cooking case.

steps.title: ילתא: for everything forbidden, something similar is permitted
steps.stepSummary: ילתא tells רב נחמן that for every forbidden thing, the Torah permitted something similar, such as liver for blood and דם טוהר for נדה.
steps.simpleTranslation: ילתא said to רב נחמן: For everything the Merciful One forbade us, He permitted something like it. He forbade blood but permitted liver. He forbade a נדה but permitted דם טוהר.
steps.whatsHappening: A new section begins. ילתא states a general rule with examples. This sets up a request she will make in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her rule: every Torah prohibition has a permitted thing that is like it. Liver is full of blood but permitted. Blood after birth, called דם טוהר, does not forbid a woman to her husband. She is building toward a matching permitted case for another prohibition.

keyTerms.meaning: Now, since (opens a reasoning)
The Merciful One (ה׳ / the Torah)
Like it, something similar
Liver
A menstruating woman
Blood of purity (bleeding after birth that does not make her impure)

steps.confusionAlert: ילתא's statement continues past this point. Her list of examples is not finished here, and her actual request comes next.

phrases.english: Yalta said to Rav Nachman:
Now, everything that the Merciful One forbade us,
He permitted us something like it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲסַר לַן דְּמָא – שְׁרָא לַן כַּבְדָּא,
phrases.english: He forbade us blood, He permitted us liver.
A menstruating woman, the blood of purity.
phrases.notes: This is shorthand: He forbade a נדה, but allowed a woman during her days of דם טוהר after birth.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרָה לֵיהּ יַלְתָּא לְרַב נַחְמָן מִכְּדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story-based section, unrelated to the tearing method.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For every Torah prohibition, a similar thing is permitted

steps.title: ילתא finishes her list and asks for a taste of meat with milk
steps.stepSummary: ילתא continues her list of forbidden things and their permitted matches, then asks to eat something that tastes like meat in milk.
steps.simpleTranslation: The fat of a domestic animal is forbidden, but the fat of a wild animal is allowed. Pig is forbidden, but the brain of the שיבוטא fish is allowed. The גירותא fish is forbidden, but a fish's tongue is allowed. A married woman is forbidden, but a woman divorced while her husband is alive is allowed. A brother's wife is forbidden, but a יבמה is allowed. A non-Jewish woman is forbidden, but a יפת תואר is allowed. So I want to eat something like meat in milk.
steps.whatsHappening: ילתא continues the list she started in step 17. She ends by asking for a taste similar to meat cooked in milk.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each pair matches something the Torah forbade with something similar it allowed, first in food and then in forbidden relationships. Her request follows from this pattern: since meat in milk is forbidden, there must be a permitted dish that tastes like it. This request sets up רב נחמן's answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Forbidden fat of a domestic animal
Wild animal, whose fat is permitted
A brother's widow when he died childless, whom the brother may marry
A captive woman taken in war, whom the Torah permits under set conditions
Meat cooked in milk, which is forbidden

phrases.english: Fat of a domestic animal: fat of a wild animal,
phrases.notes: Each pair means: this one is forbidden, but the Torah allowed the other one, which is similar.

phrases.english: pig: the brain of the shibuta fish,
giruta: the tongue of a fish.
A married woman: a divorcee while her husband is alive,
a brother's wife: a yevama,
a non-Jewish woman: a captive woman,
I want to eat meat in milk.
phrases.notes: She means something that tastes like meat in milk, not the forbidden thing itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues ילתא's list from step 17 and adds her request.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For every forbidden thing there is a permitted match, so there should be a permitted taste like meat in milk.

steps.title: רב נחמן has udders roasted for ילתא
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן tells his cooks to roast udders on a spit for her.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to the cooks: Roast udders for her on a spit.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers ילתא's request by having udders roasted. An udder holds milk, so roasted udder tastes like meat with milk but is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Udder is the permitted match for meat in milk. But רב נחמן did not tell the cooks to tear the udder first, and that sets up the גמרא's question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Cooks or butchers
Roast it on a spit
Udders

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said to the cooks:
Roast udders on a spit for her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers ילתא's request from step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Roasted udder serves as the permitted taste of meat with milk.

steps.title: Doesn't the משנה require tearing the udder?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן: the משנה says to tear the udder, but he did not say to tear it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned in the משנה: He tears it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן's instruction. The משנה says an udder must be torn open first, but he had it roasted whole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tearing lets the milk drain out. If tearing is always required, roasting the udder whole would seem wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: He tears it open, so the milk comes out

phrases.english: But we learned: He tears it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's instruction from step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן roasting udders without tearing them
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה requires tearing, and he left it out.

steps.title: Tearing is only needed for a pot
steps.stepSummary: The rule to tear the udder applies only to cooking in a pot, not to roasting.
steps.simpleTranslation: That rule is for a pot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה's tearing rule is only about cooking in a pot. Roasting is different, so רב נחמן did nothing wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a pot, the milk stays in the liquid and cooks together with the meat. On a fire the milk drips out, so there is no need to tear first.

keyTerms.meaning: Cooking pot

phrases.english: That is for a pot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the rule to one situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Tearing is needed for every kind of cooking.
steps.terutzMaskana: Tearing is needed only for cooking in a pot, not for roasting.

steps.title: The teaching's wording suggests 'only after the fact'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points to the teaching that a cooked udder is permitted. Its wording sounds like it is allowed only after the fact.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it teaches: an udder 'that one cooked' is permitted. That means after the fact yes, but from the start no?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a second challenge from the wording of an earlier teaching. 'That one cooked' sounds like it is allowed only once it already happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wording like 'that one cooked' usually describes something already done. That suggests an untorn udder is permitted only after the fact, not as a plan from the start, so how could רב נחמן order it?

keyTerms.meaning: After the fact, once it already happened
From the start, as a plan

phrases.english: But it teaches: 'that one cooked' it,
phrases.notes: This is the earlier teaching that an udder cooked in its milk is permitted.

phrases.english: after the fact yes, from the start no?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge against רב נחמן, taken from the wording of the ברייתא quoted in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's instruction to make untorn udder from the start
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The past-tense wording suggests it is permitted only after the fact.

steps.title: The wording just matches the stomach case
steps.stepSummary: Even from the start it is allowed. The teaching says 'that one cooked' only because the next case, the stomach, needs that wording.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same is true even from the start. It is worded this way because it wants to teach in the next clause: a stomach...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the udder is permitted even from the start. The 'after the fact' wording was chosen only to match the next case about a stomach, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The teaching sets two cases side by side, udder and stomach, with the same wording. The 'cooked' language fits the stomach case and was used for the udder too for neatness. So it does not limit the udder to after the fact.

keyTerms.meaning: The same law applies
Since, because of
The latter clause of a teaching
Stomach of an animal

steps.whatToRemember: Roasting an untorn udder is fine even from the start. The 'after the fact' wording only matches the next case.

phrases.english: The same is true even from the start,
and since he wants
to teach in the latter clause: a stomach
phrases.notes: The sentence keeps going on the next amud, where the stomach case is finished.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording challenge from step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the wording as matching a nearby clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The udder is permitted only after the fact.
steps.terutzMaskana: The udder is permitted even from the start. The wording follows the stomach clause.
